analysis.one_liner: Bars hospitals from forcing nurses to work beyond scheduled shifts, 12 hours a day, or 80 hours in two weeks.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 102 cosponsors from both parties but was referred to two House committees, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended Medicare rules so that hospitals, home health agencies, clinics, and other Medicare-participating providers could not force a nurse to work beyond a scheduled shift, more than 12 hours in 24, or more than 80 hours in 14 days, except during a declared emergency. It would have protected nurses who refuse or report violations from firing or discipline, let them file complaints with the Department of Health and Human Services, and imposed fines of up to $10,000 per knowing violation, with larger penalties for repeat offenders. It also directed federal agencies to study what safe maximum working hours for nurses should be.
analysis.who_benefits: Registered nurses and licensed practical nurses at Medicare-participating facilities gain a federal ceiling on forced overtime and protection from retaliation when they refuse it. Their patients benefit too: the bill's own findings cite studies linking long shifts to sharply higher error rates, so limits on fatigue-driven care protect hospital patients nationwide.

how_it_helps.text: Providers could not require a nurse to work beyond a scheduled shift, more than 12 hours in a 24-hour period, or more than 80 hours in a consecutive 14-day period, with an exception only during a declared emergency after the provider has tried to fill staffing needs by other means.

Nurses who refused mandatory overtime, filed complaints, or reported violations could not be discharged, demoted, disciplined, or reported to state licensing boards in retaliation; the Secretary had to set up a complaint procedure and investigate complaints.

The Secretary could impose civil money penalties of up to $10,000 per knowing violation, with more severe penalties for patterns of repeat violations, and publish the names of penalized providers online.

The bill cited a 2004 Health Affairs study finding nurses working shifts of 12.5 hours or more were three times more likely to commit an error, and an Institute of Medicine report recommending limits of 12 hours per day and 60 hours per week.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, home health agencies, and other Medicare-participating providers would bear the cost of ending mandatory overtime as a staffing tool — hiring more nurses, paying for voluntary overtime, or adjusting schedules. Those costs could partly show up in Medicare payment pressures or reduced scheduling flexibility. Nurses lose nothing, since voluntary overtime remains expressly allowed.

drawbacks.text: Providers would face higher staffing costs with no new Medicare funding attached; facilities already stretched for nurses might have to cut scheduled capacity or slow admissions rather than instantly hire, and rural or safety-net hospitals could feel this most.

The limits apply only to providers that participate in Medicare, so the penalty mechanism is federal money rather than a universal labor law, and the emergency exception — which excludes emergencies caused by a labor dispute or 'consistent understaffing' — still permits extended shifts during declared disasters.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill relied on studies linking fatigue to errors but directed the Secretary to conduct a further study of safe maximum hours only after enactment, meaning the 12-hour and 80-hour caps were set by legislation before the federal research it commissioned was complete.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and supported by the bill's own cited research: fewer fatigue-related medical errors and less coercive working conditions for a workforce the findings said was leaving the profession over exactly this issue. The main cost — higher staffing expenses for hospitals — is real but modest relative to the patient-safety rationale, and nine states had already enacted similar limits by the time the bill was introduced. The design is reasonable: voluntary overtime stays legal, emergencies are carved out, and enforcement runs through complaint investigation and escalating fines rather than private lawsuits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees on the day it was introduced, sent to the Health subcommittee eleven days later, and then sat there with no markup, no floor vote, and no further action until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark, a California Democrat, introduced the bill on February 14, 2005 together with Rep. Steven LaTourette, a Republican from Ohio.
It was referred to two committees — Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means — the day it was introduced, giving it two hurdles instead of one.
On February 25, 2005 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was ever recorded on the bill.
The bill attracted 102 cosponsors — 96 Democrats, 5 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but the committees never considered it, and it died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

The bill's findings noted that nine states, including California, New Jersey, and Washington, had already enacted limits on mandatory nurse overtime, leaving the rest of the country without any protection.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and other Medicare providers kept unrestricted use of mandatory overtime as a staffing tool, and continued paying nothing in penalties or added compliance costs. Nurses and patients gained nothing from the federal bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals kept forced overtime; nurses gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Pete Stark

for.name: Rep. Steven LaTourette
for.what_they_did: Joined Stark in introducing the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from day one.

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on February 25, 2005 and took no further action — no markup, no report, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic — 96 Democrats, 5 Republicans, and 1 Independent out of 102 cosponsors — with a single Republican, LaTourette, among the original sponsors; no member is recorded as opposing it, since it never came to a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have ended mandatory overtime as a staffing tool for hospitals, home health agencies, clinics, and other providers paid by Medicare, forcing them to fill shifts voluntarily or hire more staff. Their interest in defeating it ran against patient safety and nurses' working conditions, since their cost saving came from extended coerced shifts.

RNs and LPNs would have gained a federal ceiling on forced overtime plus anti-retaliation protection, and the bill's findings argued this would help retain nurses — roughly 500,000 licensed nurses were not practicing at the time.
